title: Minimax entropy production for arbitrary processes
authors: Mahran Yousef, Ben Ansbacher, David H. Wolpert
abstract: For any physical process, varying the initial distribution over its states will change the resulting expected entropy production (EP). An initial distribution that minimizes the EP of a particular process is called the prior of that process. Varying the microphysical details of the process will change its prior.We consider the following question: if an engineer wants to design a system to implement a given map, what prior should they design into the system to minimize the EP for the worst-case actual distribution? We derive the closed-form solution to this problem when the map is deterministic. We also show that for stochastic maps, a worst-case actual distribution can always be chosen to be a point mass on a single state, and that the associated minimax prior resembles a Boltzmann-Gibbs equation, and can be found by a globally convergent numerical algorithm. We also show that the associated minimax mismatch cost is the maximum uncertainty about the input that remains after observing the output. Finally, we extend the analysis to the continuous-time regime, showing that the minimax instantaneous mismatch-cost diverges, while the corresponding finite-time minimax mismatch cost has a universal short-time scaling set by the largest escape rate of the dynamics.
summary: This work develops a framework to calculate the minimax entropy production cost for physical processes, ranging from discrete maps to continuous-time dynamics. It shows that the optimal prior minimizes the worst-case cost, which is governed by the maximum uncertainty remaining after the process. The results provide universal scaling laws for the short-time behavior of this cost in Markovian systems.
main_problem: The paper determines the optimal prior distribution ($q$) for a physical system implementing a given map ($G$) that minimizes the expected thermodynamic cost (Mismatch Cost) in the worst-case scenario over all possible actual input distributions ($p$).
main_result: For deterministic maps, the minimax cost is determined by the maximum size of the input preimages (islands). For continuous-time dynamics, the instantaneous cost diverges, but the finite-time cost scales universally with the largest escape rate ($\lambda_{\max}$).
method: The analysis uses variational principles and bounds on the Mismatch Cost, decomposing the problem across equivalence classes (islands) for discrete maps and employing small-time expansions for continuous-time Markov chains.
model_or_system: The study considers general physical processes modeled by discrete stochastic maps, continuous-time Markov chains (CTMC), and abstract computational circuits (like Boolean gates). The cost function relates to entropy production and mismatch divergence.
key_observables: Minimax Mismatch Cost ($	ext{F}^*$), Shannon Entropy ($S$), Instantaneous Mismatch Cost Rate ($\dot{MMCA}$), and the maximum escape rate ($\lambda_{\max}$).
important_parameters: Time $t$, the maximum escape rate $\lambda_{\max}$, and the size of the largest preimage set $|I_y|$.
main_assumptions: For continuous time, the analysis assumes the map family $P_t$ is differentiable and the CTMC is irreducible. For discrete maps, the worst-case input is shown to be a point mass.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of minimax costs for different circuit decompositions (AND gates) and show the predicted divergence of the instantaneous mismatch-cost rate for a three-state CTMC.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from analyzing deterministic maps to stochastic maps, then extends the framework to continuous-time dynamics. It establishes the minimax cost for discrete cases, derives the divergence of the instantaneous rate, and finally solves the short-time limit for CTMCs.
why_interesting: The framework provides a rigorous information-theoretic measure (minimax cost) for quantifying the inherent thermodynamic uncertainty or irreversibility associated with implementing a physical transformation, which has implications for non-equilibrium thermodynamics.
